title: IVAM-ED: A CRP 241 Teaching Case
text:
About This Book
This book is a complete, reproducible tutorial in introductory clinical research methods built around a single published randomized trial. Every chapter uses the same dataset and the same study, so statistical concepts accumulate rather than restart. By the end you will have followed a real clinical investigation from raw data structure to published conclusion — examining the design, the analysis, the missing data, and the gap between what was planned and what was reported.
The primary language is R. All analysis is performed on a synthetic (simulated) dataset that approximates the published trial’s sample characteristics. No real participant data are used or stored anywhere in this repository.

text:
AI Assistance Disclosure
This repository, its analysis modules, and the rendered book were developed using AI-assisted agentic workflows. This section describes what was used, how it was used, and what remained the responsibility of the human instructor throughout.

0.0.1 Tools and model
GitHub Copilot Business (VS Code extension, agent mode with agentic workflow) was used for the entire development session. The underlying model was Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic), accessed through GitHub Copilot. The session was conducted under the Duke BERD Core AI Coding Pilot, Tier 2: GitHub Copilot Business with synthetic or non-sensitive data only, on a public GitHub repository.


0.0.2 What “agentic workflow” means
GitHub Copilot in agent mode allows the AI to take multi-step actions autonomously: reading files, writing and editing code, executing terminal commands, installing packages, committing to git, and pushing to GitHub. The agent did not merely suggest code — it executed the full development workflow, including:

Analyzing source PDFs to extract simulation parameters
Writing, running, debugging, and verifying the synthetic data simulation
Creating all eight analysis modules and the Quarto book infrastructure
Running security audits and rendering checks
Conducting a peer review of its own materials and implementing the recommendations



0.0.3 Human-in-the-loop: what the instructor directed
This was not autonomous AI generation. The instructor (Steve Grambow) directed every substantive decision in the session:

Case selection: The IVAM-ED trial was chosen by the instructor based on pedagogical criteria the instructor specified.
Pedagogical structure: The seven-module sequence, the learning objectives, and the decision to build a Quarto book were all instructor-directed.
Quality review: At the end of the session, the instructor requested a critical peer review of the materials, reviewed the AI’s recommendations, and directed which changes to implement.
Governance: The BERD AI pilot’s AGENTS.md operating contract governed what the agent could do autonomously (write and edit files, run terminal commands, render) versus what required instructor confirmation (git commit, git push, package installation, file deletion).
Content accuracy: The instructor reviewed the simulation parameters, the module content, and the book structure. All numbers were verified against the published source documents before use.

When the instructor was unavailable to answer interview questions (during the bootstrap phase), the agent documented its assumptions explicitly in SESSION_LOG.md and simulation-assumptions.md, and flagged them for instructor review rather than proceeding silently.


0.0.4 What the AI contributed
Speed and consistency at the implementation layer. The simulation script that would have required a half-day to write manually was drafted in minutes, with source citations embedded at the time of writing. Eight module documents were produced with consistent structure and style. Two simulation bugs were caught by automated verification and fixed through iterative debugging. The full development session — from empty repository to published Quarto book — was completed in a single working day.


0.0.5 What this disclosure is for
The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing, the American Statistical Association, and most Duke University academic integrity policies require disclosure of substantial AI assistance in educational materials. This disclosure fulfills that requirement. It is also a pedagogical statement: transparency about how materials are made is part of what the course is teaching. Students who work through Module 7 — comparing what a published analysis reported to what its protocol specified — are learning the same critical literacy that applies here.


0.0.6 Repository architecture and reproducibility foundation
This repository did not begin from a blank folder. It was initialized from the BERD AI Repository Starter — a portable scaffold developed by the Duke Biostatistics, Epidemiology, and Research Design (BERD) Core for AI-assisted clinical research analysis repositories. The starter provides:

AGENTS.md: The operating contract that governed every action taken in this session — defining what the AI could do autonomously, what required confirmation, and what was prohibited.
standards/: A set of shared, versioned standards covering data handling (data-handling.md), repository baseline requirements (repo-baseline.md), security audit procedures (security-audit.md), session start and wrap-up protocols, and — added during this project — R and Quarto teaching material quality requirements (r-quarto-teaching-materials.md) and a tutorial authoring workflow skill (r-quarto-tutorial-authoring.md).
SESSION_LOG.md: A structured session log that provides human-readable institutional memory across sessions, ensuring any future instructor or agent can recover full context from the repository files alone.

The reproducibility of this repository rests on these standards and templates, not just on the code. Anyone who clones this repository gets the same governance framework, the same operating rules, and the same documentation conventions. The Tier 2 data posture declaration, the .gitignore data exclusions, and the renv.lock package manifest are all products of standards that existed before this teaching case was built.
This architecture reflects a core principle of the BERD AI pilot: AI-assisted work is reproducible when the process is documented, not just the product.
The full session history, including every decision, file change, and command executed, is in SESSION_LOG.md. The simulation construction process is documented in simulation-assumptions.md and simulation-refinements.md. The repository itself is the audit trail. A reflective account of the full build process — case selection through deployment — is in the Process Essay appendix.

title: IVAM-ED: A CRP 241 Teaching Case
text:
The IVAM-ED Study

0.0.7 Why this study was chosen
The IVAM-ED trial — Interactive Virtual Assistant for Mental Health Promotion and Self-Care Management in Elderly with Type 2 Diabetes — was selected as the teaching case for CRP 241 for four reasons.
1. An accessible clinical question. The study asks whether a voice-activated smart speaker (Amazon Echo Dot) programmed with reminders, health tips, and educational podcasts can reduce mental distress and improve diabetes self-management in older adults. Students from any clinical background can engage with this question without specialized domain knowledge.
2. A manageable and instructive design. The trial is a conventional two-group randomized clinical trial with baseline and 12-week follow-up measurements, a single pre-specified primary outcome, and five pre-specified secondary outcomes. The design is straightforward enough to understand in full while providing rich material for every statistical concept covered in an introductory research methods course: randomization, descriptive statistics, confidence intervals, t-tests, ANCOVA, missing data, and critical appraisal.
3. Open access under Creative Commons licensing. Both the results paper and the protocol paper are published under CC-BY licenses, meaning the course repository can be made publicly available without copyright restriction. All source documents can be cited, quoted, and distributed alongside the teaching materials.
4. A rich documentation trail. The trial published a protocol and statistical analysis plan (SAP) in Trials in 2024, before the results were known. The results paper appeared in JAMA Network Open in 2026. Having both a pre-registered protocol and a published paper makes it possible to ask: did the published analysis follow the plan? That comparison — covered in Module 7 — is one of the most important critical-appraisal exercises in the course.


0.0.8 The published findings
Matzenbacher et al. (2026) enrolled 112 adults aged ≥ 65 years with type 2 diabetes at a single academic medical center in Brazil. Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive the smart speaker intervention (n = 56) or usual care (n = 56) for 12 weeks. The primary outcome was the SRQ-20 mental distress score (range 0–20; higher = more distress).
At 12 weeks, outcome data were available for 103 participants (92%). In the pre-specified fully adjusted ANCOVA, the smart speaker group had a mean SRQ-20 score 1.46 points lower than the usual care group (95% CI: −2.73 to −0.19; p = .02). The intervention was also associated with improvements in quality of life (SF-36), diabetes self-care (SCI-R), and glycemic control (HbA1c), though these secondary findings were exploratory given the absence of multiplicity adjustment. No difference was observed for perceived stress (PSS).

Source Materials and Their Roles
This repository includes six source documents: two published papers and their supplemental files. Every document plays a specific role in the teaching case.

0.0.9 The results paper

Matzenbacher LS, da Costa FL, de Barros LGB, et al. Interactive virtual assistant for health promotion among older adults with type 2 diabetes: the IVAM-ED randomized clinical trial. JAMA Network Open. 2026;9(1):e2553508. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.53508

Role: The definitive account of what was done and what was found. It provides every numerical parameter used to build the synthetic dataset: baseline demographics (Table 1), adjusted group means and 95% CIs for all outcomes (Table 2), subgroup counts (Figure 2), and the complete-case count (Results text). It is also the document students will be interpreting and critically appraising in Module 7.
Markdown extraction: source/extracted/matzenbacher-2026-ivam-ed-results-paper.md


0.0.10 The protocol and SAP paper

Da Costa FL, Matzenbacher LS, Gheno V, et al. Interactive virtual assistance for mental health promotion and self-care management in elderly with type 2 diabetes (IVAM-ED): study protocol and statistical analysis plan for a randomized controlled trial. Trials. 2024;25(1):205. doi:10.1186/s13063-024-08055-3

Role: The pre-registration document — written and published before the results were known. It describes what the investigators planned to do: the intervention, the outcome instruments, the sample size calculation (n = 112, power 90%, α = 0.05, effect size 0.68, 20% dropout assumption), the ANCOVA primary analysis, and the three pre-specified sensitivity analyses for missing data. Crucially, it specifies that secondary outcomes are exploratory and that p-values for secondary outcomes would not be the basis for conclusions.
Comparing this document to the results paper is the foundation of Module 7.
Markdown extraction: source/extracted/da-costa-2024-ivam-ed-protocol-sap.md


0.0.11 JAMA Supplement 1: Embedded protocol and SAP
The primary results paper includes a full embedded protocol and statistical analysis plan as its first supplemental appendix.
Role: A compressed reference that is easier to navigate than the Trials paper for specific SAP details — particularly the subgroup definitions, MMSE cognitive decline cutoffs, and sensitivity analysis specifications referenced in Modules 6 and 7.
Markdown extraction: source/extracted/matzenbacher-2026-supplement-1.md


0.0.12 JAMA Supplement 2: Supplemental online content
Tables and figures supporting the primary paper, including the standardized differences between study groups for all baseline characteristics (eTable 1), individual outcome supplemental tables (eTable 2), and baseline comparisons for participants with and without missing outcome data (eTable 3).
Role: Provides granular baseline balance data and the per-outcome missing-data comparison used in Module 6.
Markdown extraction: source/extracted/matzenbacher-2026-supplement-2.md


0.0.13 JAMA Supplement 3: Data sharing statement
The trial’s data availability statement.
Role: Documents that individual participant data are not publicly available, which is the direct motivation for constructing a synthetic dataset rather than using real data. The data sharing statement is part of the provenance chain: it confirms that the simulation was necessary, not a shortcut.
Markdown extraction: source/extracted/matzenbacher-2026-supplement-3.md


0.0.14 Trials Supplementary Material
The supplementary appendix to the protocol paper, including the SPIRIT checklist, detailed intervention description (28 daily messages), Brazilian-Portuguese instrument validations, and the SAP checklist.
Role: The most detailed specification of the intervention content and the instrument scoring rules. Used to verify instrument ranges in the simulation and to populate the instrument descriptions in the teaching materials.
Markdown extraction: source/extracted/da-costa-2024-supplement-1.md


0.0.15 Why include all of this? Transparency and reproducibility
Combining the results paper, the pre-registered protocol, and all supplemental materials in one repository reflects a principle that is increasingly central to clinical research: reproducibility requires documentation, not just code.
A simulation that correctly reproduces the published numbers without disclosing its source would be a black box. A simulation with all sources linked, all parameters cited, and all deviations documented is:

Auditable: instructors and students can verify every number.
Correctable: if a parameter was approximated incorrectly, the source document shows what the correct value should be.
Pedagogically complete: students can trace the path from published summary statistic to simulated data value to analysis output to interpreted conclusion.

This also models a research practice that applies beyond teaching: when you publish analysis code, include the data source, the provenance chain, and the decisions that shaped the analysis.

Repository Structure and How It Was Built

0.0.16 Initial setup
This repository was initialized using the BERD AI Repository Starter — a portable scaffold for AI-assisted clinical research analysis repositories developed by the Duke Biostatistics, Epidemiology, and Research Design (BERD) Core as part of a GitHub Copilot pilot program. The starter provides:

AGENTS.md: an operating contract for AI coding tools that specifies what an AI agent may do autonomously versus what requires confirmation.
standards/: a set of shared standards covering data handling, session logging, security, and teaching material quality.
A bootstrap procedure that interviews the user and generates the baseline repository files.

The bootstrap interview established:

Tier 2 — GitHub Copilot Business, synthetic or non-sensitive data only, GitHub remote (per the BERD pilot governance framework).
Primary language: R with Quarto and renv.
Data posture: synthetic/simulated only; no real participant data at any stage.

Full bootstrap and session history is in SESSION_LOG.md.


0.0.17 Source document extraction
All six source documents (PDFs and one DOCX) were converted to Markdown at initialization using miyo parse (for PDFs) and pandoc (for the DOCX file). The Markdown extractions in source/extracted/ serve as the working reference for every simulation parameter and every teaching material claim. They are not modified from the extracted output; any corrections would be flagged as deviations from the source.


0.0.18 The synthetic dataset
The synthetic dataset is generated by R/simulate-ivam-ed.R using the following strategy:

Moment matching. For each variable, we chose a probability distribution whose mean and standard deviation match the published Table 1 values. This is the simplest defensible approach when only summary statistics are available.
ANCOVA-generating model. Follow-up outcomes were simulated using: \[y_{12,i} = \alpha + \tau \cdot \text{group}_i + \beta \cdot (y_{0,i} - \bar{y}_0) + \varepsilon_i\] where \(\tau\) is taken directly from the published Table 2 baseline-adjusted mean differences, \(\beta = 0.70\) (a standard test-retest correlation for 12-week clinical outcomes), and \(\alpha\) equals the published control-group adjusted mean.
MAR missingness. The 9 missing participants (5 control, 4 intervention) are assigned deterministically — those with the highest baseline SRQ-20 within each group — reflecting a clinically plausible missing-at-random mechanism.

Full simulation parameter documentation is in the Simulation Assumptions appendix.


0.0.19 Simulation refinement
The simulation required two debugging cycles before producing correct output. Both bugs were caught by the verification summary printed at the end of the script:
Bug 1 (ANCOVA centering): The intercept was initially calibrated at the control group’s baseline mean rather than the grand mean, causing the treatment effect (\(\tau\)) to be almost entirely offset by chance baseline imbalance in the simulated data. Fix: center the baseline covariate at the grand mean so that \(\alpha\) directly equals the published control-group adjusted mean.
Bug 2 (missingness split): A probabilistic logistic model for missingness assigned 1 and 8 missing participants to the two groups instead of the target 4 and 5. Fix: deterministic rank-based selection within each group.
After both fixes, the ANCOVA recovers an adjusted MD of −1.19 (published: −1.28), which is close enough for a teaching dataset. The full debugging narrative — including the mathematical diagnosis for each bug — is in the Simulation Refinements appendix. This document is part of the teaching case: it illustrates the verify–diagnose–fix–re-verify cycle that applies to any quantitative analysis.

title: IVAM-ED: A CRP 241 Teaching Case
text:
Learning Objectives
After completing all seven modules, students will be able to:

0.0.20 Data management

Load an R data frame, inspect its structure, and identify variable types.
Recognize the _0 (baseline) and _12 (follow-up) suffix convention for repeated measurements.
Count and characterize missing values and explain why missingness matters.



0.0.21 Descriptive statistics

Compute means, standard deviations, medians, frequencies, and percentages.
Construct and interpret a baseline characteristics table (Table 1).
Explain why significance tests of baseline differences are inappropriate in a randomized trial and use standardized mean differences instead.



0.0.22 Data visualization

Construct histograms, box plots, and individual trajectory plots in ggplot2.
Describe distributional features (skewness, outliers, floor/ceiling effects) from a plot.
Identify regression to the mean as a visual pattern in pre-post data.



0.0.23 Estimation and inference

Compute group means, mean changes from baseline, and between-group mean differences with 95% confidence intervals.
Conduct an independent-samples t-test and interpret the p-value correctly.
Distinguish within-group change (not the treatment effect) from the between-group difference (the treatment effect).



0.0.24 Regression and ANCOVA

Fit a linear regression model using lm() and interpret each coefficient.
Explain why adjusting for baseline increases precision without introducing bias.
Calculate adjusted means using predict() and compare them to observed means.
Reproduce the primary analysis of a published randomized trial.



0.0.25 Missing data

Describe the MCAR, MAR, and MNAR mechanisms and their implications.
Conduct a complete-case analysis and state its assumptions.
Apply a BOCF sensitivity analysis.
Run multiple imputation with mice and pool results using Rubin’s rules.



0.0.26 Interpretation and critical appraisal

Distinguish statistical significance from clinical significance using MCID.
Identify a trial’s pre-specified primary outcome and label secondary outcomes as exploratory.
Apply Bonferroni correction and explain what changes.
Compare a published analysis to its pre-registered protocol and evaluate identified deviations.

title: IVAM-ED: A CRP 241 Teaching Case
text:
Chapter Guide
Each chapter addresses a distinct methodological question and is designed to take approximately 45–90 minutes for a student working independently.

0.0.27 Module 1 — Data Setup and Inspection
What are the data? What do the variables mean? Who is missing?
Introduces the synthetic dataset: variable types, instrument descriptions and score directions, group assignment, and the 9 participants with missing follow-up data. Establishes the working dataset used in all subsequent modules.
Key concepts: data frames, variable labels, binary vs. continuous variables, missing values, range checks.


0.0.28 Module 2 — Descriptive Statistics and Baseline Characteristics
Who was enrolled? Are the two groups similar at baseline?
Constructs Table 1 using gtsummary. Introduces standardized mean differences as the appropriate measure of baseline balance and explains the CONSORT rationale for omitting p-values from Table 1 in a randomized trial.
Key concepts: means and SDs, frequencies and percentages, Table 1, standardized mean differences, CONSORT reporting guidelines.


0.0.29 Module 3 — Data Visualization
What do the outcome distributions look like? Do individuals improve?
Builds four types of visualizations: a baseline histogram with density overlay, faceted box plots with jittered individual points, individual trajectory plots with group mean lines, and a side-by-side floor/ceiling check. Introduces regression to the mean as a visual concept.
Key concepts: histograms, box plots, jitter plots, trajectory plots, floor and ceiling effects, regression to the mean.


0.0.30 Module 4 — Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
How much did each group change? How different were they at follow-up?
Computes group means at both time points and the within-group change. Derives the Welch t-interval formula before applying t.test(). Builds a forest plot for all five outcomes. Emphasizes the distinction between within-group change and the randomized between-group comparison.
Key concepts: mean difference, standard error, 95% confidence interval, Welch t-test, p-value interpretation, forest plots.


0.0.31 Module 5 — Linear Regression and ANCOVA
Does adjusting for baseline change the estimate and its precision?
Fits the pre-specified ANCOVA using lm(). Demonstrates the precision gain from baseline adjustment by comparing CI widths. Introduces adjusted means via predict(). Extends to the fully adjusted model and replicates Table 2.
Key concepts: linear regression, ANCOVA, treatment coefficient, adjusted means, grand mean centering, efficiency gain from covariate adjustment.


0.0.32 Module 6 — Missing Data
Does it matter how we handle the 9 participants with missing follow-up data?
Compares three approaches: complete-case analysis, baseline-observation-carried forward (BOCF), and multiple imputation with the mice package. Visualizes all three estimates on a forest plot and assesses the robustness of the primary conclusion.
Key concepts: MCAR / MAR / MNAR, complete-case analysis, BOCF, multiple imputation, Rubin’s rules, sensitivity analysis.


0.0.33 Module 7 — Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
Is the result clinically meaningful? Did the paper follow its own plan?
Introduces the minimum clinically important difference (MCID) and visualizes the CI against that threshold. Applies Bonferroni correction to the five outcomes. Conducts a structured protocol-to-publication comparison identifying four specific deviations between the Da Costa 2024 protocol and the Matzenbacher 2026 paper.
Key concepts: clinical significance, effect size, Cohen’s d, MCID, multiplicity correction, confirmatory vs. exploratory inference, protocol adherence.

Work sequentially. Each module depends on the data and concepts established in the previous one. Module 2 loads the working dataset created by Module 1; Modules 3–8 use the same completers object.
Changing the seed. set.seed(241) in R/simulate-ivam-ed.R produces identical data for all students. To assign different datasets to different student groups, change the seed number before distributing. Document the seed you used in your course materials.
Answer key. The Answer Key appendix provides worked solutions. These answers are based on set.seed(241) — update key values if you distribute a different seed.
Simulation documentation. See the Simulation Assumptions appendix for the full parameter table (every number linked to a paper table), and Simulation Refinements for the debugging narrative (useful for advanced students or instructor background). 2.2 The IVAM-ED Study
The IVAM-ED trial evaluated whether a voice-activated smart speaker (Amazon Echo Dot) could improve mental health and diabetes self-management among older adults with type 2 diabetes. Researchers in Brazil randomly assigned 112 adults (age ≥ 65) to either:

Intervention: Use a smart speaker at home for 12 weeks. The device was programmed with reminders, health messages, and educational podcasts.
Usual care: Continue with standard diabetes management and no device.

The primary outcome was the SRQ-20 score (Self-Reporting Questionnaire, 0–20), a measure of mental distress. Lower scores mean less distress.

Important: We are working with a synthetic (simulated) dataset — not real participant data. The dataset was constructed to approximate the published summary statistics. See simulation-assumptions.md for how it was built and what assumptions were made.

Note



Why the data are always the same: set.seed()
At the top of simulate-ivam-ed.R you will find set.seed(241). This locks R’s random number generator to a fixed starting point. R’s “randomness” is actually a deterministic algorithm — a mathematical formula that produces a long sequence of numbers that look random but are completely determined by the starting value (the seed). Given the same seed, R will always generate the same sequence.
This is deliberate for a teaching dataset: every student gets identical data, so results are comparable and answers are verifiable.
Try it yourself: Open R/simulate-ivam-ed.R, change set.seed(241) to set.seed(999), source the script, and re-run this module. Your Table 1 means will shift slightly, the primary ANCOVA result may change in magnitude, and it may or may not remain statistically significant — illustrating that any single study is one realization of a random process.

3.3 1. Univariate Summaries
Before building a grouped table, it helps to look at the whole sample together. This gives you a feel for the data and catches obvious problems (values out of range, unexpected distributions).

3.4 2. Table 1: Baseline Characteristics by Randomized Group
The standard way to present baseline characteristics in a clinical trial is a Table 1: one column per group, with each row showing a baseline variable.
We use gtsummary::tbl_summary() to build this table. The package automatically selects appropriate statistics (mean ± SD for continuous variables, n (%) for categorical variables) and formats the output for publication.

# Prepare a clean analysis dataset for Table 1
# Rename group to a labeled factor so the column headers read clearly
dat_t1 <- dat |>
  select(
    group_label,
    # Demographics
    age, female, edu_years, income_wages,
    # Clinical
    dm_duration_y, insulin,
    # Comorbidities
    hx_depression, hx_anxiety, cognitive_decline,
    # Baseline scores
    mmse_0, srq20_0, sci_r_0, pss_0, sf36_0, hba1c_0
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Convert binary integers to labeled factors for cleaner table display
    female            = factor(female,            levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("Female", "Male")),
    insulin           = factor(insulin,           levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("Yes", "No")),
    hx_depression     = factor(hx_depression,     levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("Yes", "No")),
    hx_anxiety        = factor(hx_anxiety,        levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("Yes", "No")),
    cognitive_decline = factor(cognitive_decline, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("Yes", "No"))
  )

# Build the table
tbl_summary(
  dat_t1,
  by = group_label,
  label = list(
    age               ~ "Age, years",
    female            ~ "Female sex",
    edu_years         ~ "Education, years",
    income_wages      ~ "Income, min. wages/month",
    dm_duration_y     ~ "Diabetes duration, years",
    insulin           ~ "Insulin use",
    hx_depression     ~ "History of depression",
    hx_anxiety        ~ "History of anxiety",
    cognitive_decline ~ "Cognitive decline screening (positive)",
    mmse_0            ~ "MMSE score (0–30)",
    srq20_0           ~ "SRQ-20 score (0–20)",
    sci_r_0           ~ "SCI-R score (0–56)",
    pss_0             ~ "PSS score (0–40)",
    sf36_0            ~ "SF-36 score (0–100)",
    hba1c_0           ~ "HbA1c, %"
  ),
  statistic = list(
    all_continuous()  ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
    all_categorical() ~ "{n} ({p}%)"
  ),
  digits = list(
    all_continuous() ~ 1
  ),
  missing = "no"   # missing data handled separately
) |>
  add_overall() |>
  modify_header(label ~ "**Characteristic**") |>
  modify_spanning_header(c("stat_1", "stat_2") ~ "**Randomized group**") |>

3.5 3. Interpreting Baseline Balance

3.5.1 3a. What “balanced” means in a randomized trial
After randomization, we compare baseline characteristics between groups. In a perfectly balanced trial, every characteristic would be identical across groups. In practice, small differences always occur by chance, even with proper randomization.
The key question is: are any of the differences large enough to matter?

# Calculate the mean difference between groups for each continuous outcome
# and the standardized mean difference (SMD)
dat |>
  group_by(group_label) |>
  summarise(
    age_mean       = mean(age),
    srq20_mean     = mean(srq20_0),
    hba1c_mean     = mean(hba1c_0),
    sf36_mean      = mean(sf36_0),
    pss_mean       = mean(pss_0),
    sci_r_mean     = mean(sci_r_0)
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-group_label, names_to = "variable", values_to = "mean") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = group_label, values_from = mean) |>
  mutate(difference = round(`Smart speaker` - `Usual care`, 2))

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  variable   `Usual care` `Smart speaker` difference

1 age_mean          72.3            72.6        0.38

3 hba1c_mean         7.89            7.34      -0.55
4 sf36_mean         47.8            52.3        4.48
5 pss_mean          23.7            22.1       -1.67
6 sci_r_mean        35.5            38.3        2.84




3.5.2 3b. Why we do NOT test for statistical significance at baseline
You may notice that Table 1 in our simulated output (and in most published trials) does not include a p-value column. This is intentional, and it is one of the most important conventions in clinical trial reporting.
The reason: In a properly randomized trial, any baseline difference between groups arose by chance — by definition, because we randomized. Testing whether a baseline difference is “statistically significant” asks: “Is this difference too large to be due to chance?” But we already know it is due to chance (the randomization). The test cannot tell us anything informative.
What matters instead is whether the difference is clinically meaningful — large enough to affect the outcome, regardless of its p-value. A large p-value does not mean a baseline imbalance is unimportant; it means only that the sample was too small to detect it with confidence.






Important



CONSORT reporting guideline: Table 1 in a randomized trial should show baseline characteristics but should not include p-values for between-group comparisons. This is stated explicitly in the CONSORT 2010 guidelines (Schulz et al., 2010, BMJ).




3.5.3 3c. Standardized mean differences
A more informative measure of baseline balance is the standardized mean difference (SMD): the group difference divided by the pooled standard deviation. Values below 0.1 are generally considered small (good balance); values above 0.2 may warrant adjustment in the primary analysis.

# gtsummary can add SMDs directly to the Table 1

  by = group_label,
  statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})"),
  digits    = list(all_continuous() ~ 1),
  missing   = "no"
) |>

  modify_header(estimate ~ "**SMD**") |>

title: 4  Module 3: Data Visualization
text:
4.1 Overview
Visualization is not decoration — it is analysis. Plots reveal distributional features (skewness, outliers, floor effects), patterns across groups, and individual variability that summary statistics conceal.
By the end of this module you should be able to:

title: 4  Module 3: Data Visualization
text:
Plot the distribution of a continuous variable with a histogram and density curve.
Compare distributions between two groups with side-by-side box plots.
Visualize change from baseline using an individual-trajectory plot.
Describe what each plot tells you about the data that a table cannot.

title: 4  Module 3: Data Visualization
text:
4.2 Setup

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # combines multiple ggplot panels into one figure


dat <- readRDS("../data/ivam_working.rds")

# Completers only (those with follow-up data) — used in several plots
completers <- filter(dat, missing_12wk == 0)

title: 4  Module 3: Data Visualization
section: 4.3 1. Distribution of the Primary Outcome at Baseline
text:
4.3 1. Distribution of the Primary Outcome at Baseline
The SRQ-20 is the primary outcome: a 20-item mental-distress questionnaire. Before looking at treatment effects, we should understand what its distribution looks like in this sample.

ggplot(dat, aes(x = srq20_0)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#4472C4", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(count)), color = "#C00000", linewidth = 0.8,
               adjust = 1.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 20, 2), limits = c(-0.5, 20.5)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Distribution of SRQ-20 Score at Baseline",
    subtitle = "All 112 enrolled participants",
    x        = "SRQ-20 score (0 = no distress, 20 = maximum distress)",
    y        = "Number of participants",
    caption  = "Red curve: smoothed density overlay"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)














Note



What to notice:

The distribution is right-skewed: most participants have low scores but a tail of participants have scores above 10.
There is no sharp floor at 0 (the distribution is not dominated by zeros), meaning mental distress is present at a detectable level throughout this sample.
The SRQ-20 is an integer sum score — that is why the bars fall at whole numbers.

title: 4  Module 3: Data Visualization
text:
4.4 2. Baseline Distributions by Group
Do the two groups look similar at baseline? We would hope so — randomization should produce roughly equivalent groups, but it does not guarantee perfect balance in every variable.

# Reshape to long format so we can facet across all five outcomes at once
outcomes_long <- dat |>
  select(participant_id, group_label, srq20_0, sf36_0, sci_r_0, pss_0, hba1c_0) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(srq20_0, sf36_0, sci_r_0, pss_0, hba1c_0),
    names_to  = "outcome",
    values_to = "score"
  ) |>
  mutate(outcome = recode(outcome,
    srq20_0 = "SRQ-20\n(0–20, higher = worse distress)",
    sf36_0  = "SF-36\n(0–100, higher = better QoL)",
    sci_r_0 = "SCI-R\n(0–56, higher = better self-care)",
    pss_0   = "PSS\n(0–40, higher = more stress)",
    hba1c_0 = "HbA1c %\n(lower = better glycemic control)"
  ))

ggplot(outcomes_long, aes(x = group_label, y = score, fill = group_label)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = 21, outlier.size = 1.5,
               width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.3, size = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Usual care" = "#ED7D31", "Smart speaker" = "#4472C4")) +
  facet_wrap(~ outcome, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title   = "Baseline Outcome Distributions by Randomized Group",
    x       = NULL,
    y       = "Score",
    fill    = NULL,
    caption = "Points are individual participants; box shows median and IQR"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 9))














Note



What to notice:

The groups look broadly similar across all five outcomes — this is the expected result of randomization.
The SRQ-20 box for the smart speaker group is shifted slightly upward relative to the usual care group (the intervention group started with slightly higher distress). This is chance imbalance; the ANCOVA adjustment in Module 5 will account for it.
The jittered individual points show the spread within each group. Box plots can hide multimodal distributions or extreme outliers that individual points reveal.

title: 4  Module 3: Data Visualization
text:
4.5 3. Change from Baseline: Individual Trajectories
The most informative visualization for a pre-post trial is an individual trajectory plot: one line per participant, connecting their baseline score to their follow-up score. This shows both the direction and magnitude of change for each person, not just the group average.

# Reshape to long: one row per participant per time point
srq20_long <- completers |>
  select(participant_id, group_label, srq20_0, srq20_12) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(srq20_0, srq20_12),
    names_to  = "timepoint",
    values_to = "srq20"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    timepoint = recode(timepoint,
      srq20_0  = "Baseline\n(Week −1)",
      srq20_12 = "Follow-up\n(Week 12)"
    ),
    timepoint = factor(timepoint,
      levels = c("Baseline\n(Week −1)", "Follow-up\n(Week 12)"))
  )

ggplot(srq20_long,
       aes(x = timepoint, y = srq20, group = participant_id, color = group_label)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.2) +
  # Add group mean lines on top
  stat_summary(aes(group = group_label), fun = mean,
               geom = "line", linewidth = 1.5, alpha = 0.9) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = group_label), fun = mean,
               geom = "point", size = 3, shape = 18) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Usual care" = "#ED7D31", "Smart speaker" = "#4472C4")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 20), breaks = seq(0, 20, 4)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Individual SRQ-20 Trajectories: Baseline to 12 Weeks",
    subtitle = "Thin lines = individual participants; thick lines = group means",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "SRQ-20 score (higher = more distress)",
    color    = NULL,
    caption  = "Completers only (n = 103)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")














Note



What to notice:

Color key: orange lines = Usual care group; blue lines = Smart speaker (intervention) group. The thick lines are group means; thin lines are individual participants.
Both group means decline from baseline to follow-up — a drop in SRQ-20 means less distress, which is an improvement.
The smart speaker group mean (blue thick line) drops further than the usual care group mean (orange thick line). The vertical distance between the two thick lines at week 12 represents the unadjusted mean difference.
Individual variability is large: some participants in both groups get worse, not better. The group-level treatment effect is a central tendency, not a guarantee for any individual.
The crossing thin lines reveal that participants who started with high scores tend to show larger decreases — this is regression to the mean, which the ANCOVA model in Module 5 will address.

title: 4  Module 3: Data Visualization
text:
4.6 4. Comparing All Outcomes at Follow-Up
A side-by-side comparison of follow-up distributions across all outcomes gives an overview of where the intervention had an effect and where it did not.

followup_long <- completers |>
  select(participant_id, group_label,
         srq20_12, sf36_12, sci_r_12, pss_12, hba1c_12) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(srq20_12, sf36_12, sci_r_12, pss_12, hba1c_12),
    names_to  = "outcome",
    values_to = "score"
  ) |>
  mutate(outcome = recode(outcome,
    srq20_12 = "SRQ-20 (primary)\nhigher = worse distress",
    sf36_12  = "SF-36\nhigher = better QoL",
    sci_r_12 = "SCI-R\nhigher = better self-care",
    pss_12   = "PSS\nhigher = more stress",
    hba1c_12 = "HbA1c %\nlower = better glycemic control"
  ))

ggplot(followup_long, aes(x = group_label, y = score, fill = group_label)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = 21, outlier.size = 1.5, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.3, size = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Usual care" = "#ED7D31", "Smart speaker" = "#4472C4")) +
  facet_wrap(~ outcome, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title   = "Outcome Distributions at 12-Week Follow-Up by Group",
    x       = NULL,
    y       = "Score",
    fill    = NULL,
    caption = "Points are individual participants; box shows median and IQR"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 9))














Note



Direction guide for comparing groups:

SRQ-20: Smart speaker group should be lower (less distress is better).
SF-36 and SCI-R: Smart speaker group should be higher (more is better).
PSS: Smart speaker group should be lower (less stress is better).
HbA1c: Smart speaker group should be lower (lower % is better glycemic control).

The published trial found statistically significant effects on SRQ-20, SF-36, SCI-R, and HbA1c, but not on PSS (the CI for PSS crossed zero). Look at your plots: do any of the comparisons look visually similar (no clear separation), even if a difference exists?

title: 4  Module 3: Data Visualization
text:
4.7 5. Floor and Ceiling Effects
A floor effect occurs when many participants score at or near the lowest possible value — they cannot get lower, so the instrument cannot detect further improvement. A ceiling effect is the reverse. Either distorts the analysis.

p_srq <- ggplot(completers, aes(x = srq20_12, fill = group_label)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, position = "identity", alpha = 0.65) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.5, 20.5), breaks = seq(0, 20, 4)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Usual care" = "#ED7D31", "Smart speaker" = "#4472C4")) +
  labs(title = "SRQ-20 at 12 weeks", x = "Score", y = "Count", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_sf36 <- ggplot(completers, aes(x = sf36_12, fill = group_label)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, position = "identity", alpha = 0.65) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Usual care" = "#ED7D31", "Smart speaker" = "#4472C4")) +
  labs(title = "SF-36 at 12 weeks", x = "Score", y = "Count", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_srq + p_sf36 +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "Follow-Up Distributions: Checking for Floor and Ceiling Effects",
    caption = "A pile-up of scores at 0 (SRQ-20) or 100 (SF-36) would indicate a floor or ceiling effect"
  )














Note



What to look for: Are scores piled up against the boundary of the scale? In the IVAM-ED data, mean SRQ-20 at follow-up is around 7, well above the floor of 0, so floor effects are not a major concern. The SF-36 mean is around 55, well below the ceiling of 100.

5.1 Overview
This module moves from description to inference. We quantify the treatment effect using means, mean differences, 95% confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests — and we examine the critical distinction between two types of comparison that are often confused:
In a randomized trial, only the between-group difference is the legitimate estimate of the treatment effect. Within-group change is confounded by everything that happens to participants over time (natural history, regression to the mean, seasonal effects).
By the end of this module you should be able to:

text:
5.3 1. Group Means at Each Time Point
Start by computing the unadjusted group means for the primary outcome (SRQ-20) at baseline and at follow-up.

# Mean and SD for SRQ-20 at each time point, by group
completers |>
  group_by(group_label) |>

5.4 2. Within-Group Change
For each group, we can calculate the mean change from baseline to follow-up. This tells us: on average, how much did participants in this group change?

completers |>
  mutate(srq20_change = srq20_12 - srq20_0) |>   # negative = improved (less distress)
  group_by(group_label) |>
  summarise(
    n           = n(),
    mean_change = round(mean(srq20_change), 2),
    sd_change   = round(sd(srq20_change),   2),
    se_change   = round(sd(srq20_change) / sqrt(n()), 3),
    ci_lo       = round(mean(srq20_change) - qt(0.975, df = n() - 1) * sd(srq20_change) / sqrt(n()), 2),
    ci_hi       = round(mean(srq20_change) + qt(0.975, df = n() - 1) * sd(srq20_change) / sqrt(n()), 2)
  ) |>
  mutate(ci = paste0("(", ci_lo, ", ", ci_hi, ")")) |>
  select(group_label, n, mean_change, sd_change, ci)

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  group_label       n mean_change sd_change ci            
  <fct>         <int>       <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>         
1 Usual care       51        0.55      2.65 (-0.2, 1.29)  
2 Smart speaker    52       -0.96      2.33 (-1.61, -0.31)








Warning



Why within-group change is not the treatment effect.
Both groups may show mean improvement over 12 weeks for reasons unrelated to the intervention:

Regression to the mean: participants with high distress at enrollment often have somewhat lower distress later, regardless of treatment.
Natural history: diabetes and mental distress can fluctuate over time.
Attention effects: being enrolled in a study and followed by a research team may itself reduce distress (the Hawthorne effect).

The within-group change in the control group estimates everything that happens to patients over time without the intervention. Only the difference between the two groups’ changes isolates the intervention’s contribution.

text:
5.5 3. Between-Group Difference (Unadjusted)
The between-group mean difference at follow-up is the primary estimate of the treatment effect — how much better (or worse) the intervention group did compared to the control group, on average.

# Unadjusted mean difference at follow-up (intervention - control)
means <- completers |>
  group_by(group_label) |>
  summarise(
    n    = n(),
    mean = mean(srq20_12),
    sd   = sd(srq20_12)
  )

n_int  <- means$n   [means$group_label == "Smart speaker"]
n_ctrl <- means$n   [means$group_label == "Usual care"]
m_int  <- means$mean[means$group_label == "Smart speaker"]
m_ctrl <- means$mean[means$group_label == "Usual care"]
sd_int <- means$sd  [means$group_label == "Smart speaker"]
sd_ctrl<- means$sd  [means$group_label == "Usual care"]

# Unadjusted mean difference and 95% CI (Welch t-interval)
md     <- m_int - m_ctrl
se_md  <- sqrt(sd_int^2 / n_int + sd_ctrl^2 / n_ctrl)
df_welch <- (sd_int^2/n_int + sd_ctrl^2/n_ctrl)^2 /
            ((sd_int^2/n_int)^2/(n_int-1) + (sd_ctrl^2/n_ctrl)^2/(n_ctrl-1))
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = df_welch)

cat(sprintf("Unadjusted mean difference (int - ctrl): %.2f\n", md))

Unadjusted mean difference (int - ctrl): -0.47

cat(sprintf("Standard error:                          %.3f\n", se_md))

Standard error:                          0.673

cat(sprintf("95%% CI:                                  (%.2f, %.2f)\n",
    md - t_crit * se_md, md + t_crit * se_md))

95% CI:                                  (-1.80, 0.87)

cat(sprintf("Degrees of freedom (Welch):              %.1f\n", df_welch))

Degrees of freedom (Welch):              100.9








Note



Interpreting the sign: SRQ-20 measures distress (higher = worse). A negative mean difference (intervention minus control) means the intervention group had lower distress — an improvement. The published baseline-adjusted MD was −1.28 (95% CI: −2.51 to −0.04). Your unadjusted estimate may be closer to zero because it does not account for the baseline imbalance (the intervention group started slightly higher).

text:
5.6 4. Hypothesis Test: Independent-Samples t-Test
A hypothesis test asks: “If the intervention truly had no effect, how often would we see a mean difference this large (or larger) by chance alone?”
The null hypothesis (H₀): the population mean SRQ-20 at 12 weeks is the same in both groups. The alternative hypothesis (H₁): the means differ.

# Two-sample t-test with Welch correction (does not assume equal variances)
t_result <- t.test(
  srq20_12 ~ group_label,
  data    = completers,
  var.equal = FALSE   # Welch t-test; safer default when group SDs may differ
)

# Explicitly name which group is subtracted from which to avoid silent ordering errors

    m_smart - m_usual))

Mean difference: -0.466 (Smart speaker minus Usual care)








Note



Reading the p-value: A p-value below 0.05 (the conventional threshold) means that, if there were truly no treatment effect, we would observe a difference this large less than 5% of the time by chance. A p-value above 0.05 does not mean the treatment has no effect — it means the data are consistent with no effect, but do not rule it out either. With n = 103, the trial has limited power to detect small effects.
The published trial used ANCOVA (not a t-test) as the primary analysis. The ANCOVA estimate will be more precise — we will fit it in Module 5.

text:
5.7 5. All Secondary Outcomes
The trial had five secondary outcomes. We test all of them here using the same unadjusted t-test approach, but note that we will not adjust for multiple comparisons — and we need to be careful about interpreting the results.

# Helper function: run a t-test and return a tidy one-row summary
ttest_summary <- function(data, outcome_var, outcome_label, better_dir) {
  formula <- as.formula(paste(outcome_var, "~ group_label"))
  res <- t.test(formula, data = data, var.equal = FALSE)

  # Difference is Smart speaker minus Usual care
  est <- res$estimate
  md  <- est[grep("Smart", names(est))] - est[grep("Usual", names(est))]
  if (length(md) == 0) md <- diff(res$estimate)   # fallback

  tibble(
    Outcome      = outcome_label,
    `Better direction`  = better_dir,
    `MD (Int − Ctrl)` = round(as.numeric(md), 3),
    `95% CI`     = sprintf("(%.2f, %.2f)", res$conf.int[1], res$conf.int[2]),
    `p-value`    = round(res$p.value, 3)
  )
}

outcomes_table <- bind_rows(
  ttest_summary(completers, "srq20_12",

text:
5.8 6. Visualizing the Treatment Effect with a Forest Plot
A forest plot shows the mean difference and 95% CI for each outcome on the same scale, making it easy to compare effect sizes and their precision.

# Compute MDs and CIs for all outcomes
forest_data <- bind_rows(
  lapply(
    list(
      list(var = "srq20_12", label = "SRQ-20 (primary)",          direction = -1),
      list(var = "sf36_12",  label = "SF-36 (quality of life)",   direction =  1),
      list(var = "sci_r_12", label = "SCI-R (self-care)",         direction =  1),
      list(var = "pss_12",   label = "PSS (perceived stress)",    direction = -1),
      list(var = "hba1c_12", label = "HbA1c % (glycemic control)",direction = -1)
    ),
    function(o) {
      res <- t.test(
        as.formula(paste(o$var, "~ group_label")),
        data = completers, var.equal = FALSE
      )
      est <- res$estimate
      md  <- est[grep("Smart", names(est))] - est[grep("Usual", names(est))]
      if (length(md) == 0) md <- diff(res$estimate)
      tibble(
        label    = o$label,
        md       = as.numeric(md),
        ci_lo    = res$conf.int[1],
        ci_hi    = res$conf.int[2],
        p        = res$p.value,
        sig      = p < 0.05
      )
    }
  )
) |>
  # Flip sign for outcomes where negative = better so "favors intervention" is always right
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(label)))

ggplot(forest_data, aes(x = md, xmin = ci_lo, xmax = ci_hi, y = label,
                        color = sig)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbarh(height = 0.25, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5, shape = 18) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#4472C4", "FALSE" = "#999999"),
                     labels = c("TRUE" = "p < 0.05", "FALSE" = "p ≥ 0.05"),
                     name   = NULL) +
  labs(
    title   = "Unadjusted Mean Differences at 12 Weeks (Smart Speaker − Usual Care)",
    subtitle = "Negative = favors intervention for SRQ-20, PSS, HbA1c; Positive = favors for SF-36, SCI-R",
    x       = "Mean difference (intervention minus control)",
    y       = NULL,
    caption = "Unadjusted two-sample t-test; ANCOVA estimates in Module 5"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")














Note



Reading the forest plot: Each point is the estimated mean difference; the horizontal bar is the 95% CI. A CI that does not cross zero (dashed line) means the result is statistically significant at α = 0.05. Blue points are significant; grey are not. Note that the PSS confidence interval likely crosses zero — consistent with the published finding that perceived stress was not a statistically significant outcome.

Within-group vs. between-group. The smart speaker group improved on average from baseline to 12 weeks (within-group change). The usual care group also improved. title: 6  Module 5: Linear Regression and ANCOVA
text:
6.3 1. Why Adjust for Baseline?
When participants are randomized, the two groups are expected to be balanced at baseline on average — but in any finite sample, chance imbalances occur. In our simulated data (and the real IVAM-ED trial), the intervention group started with a slightly higher SRQ-20 score than the control group.
Two consequences of baseline imbalance:

The unadjusted mean difference is biased. If the intervention group starts higher, regression to the mean will push them down more, even without a real treatment effect. Adjusting for baseline removes this confounding.
Adjusting for baseline increases precision. Because baseline scores are strongly correlated with follow-up scores, including the baseline as a covariate reduces residual variance. This makes confidence intervals narrower and tests more powerful — for free, without collecting additional data.


# How strongly correlated are baseline and follow-up SRQ-20?
with(completers, round(cor(srq20_0, srq20_12, use = "complete.obs"), 3))

[1] 0.748








Note



Interpreting the correlation: A value near 0.7 means that knowing a participant’s baseline score explains about 49% of the variance in their follow-up score (r² = 0.70² ≈ 0.49). Including the baseline in the regression model can therefore reduce the residual variance by roughly half, which substantially narrows the confidence interval for the treatment effect.

Interpreting the group coefficient (the treatment effect):

This is the estimated mean difference in SRQ-20 at 12 weeks between the intervention and control groups, holding baseline SRQ-20 constant.

A 1.1-point baseline imbalance almost completely offset the specified treatment effect, making the raw follow-up means nearly identical between groups. The fix — centering the baseline covariate at the grand mean — is exactly what this section demonstrates: adjusted means are estimated at the grand mean, not the group mean. 6.5 2b. Check Model Assumptions
Before interpreting ANCOVA results, verify the two key linear regression assumptions: residuals are approximately normally distributed, and residual variance is roughly constant across fitted values (homoscedasticity).

# Standard residual diagnostic plots for the baseline-adjusted ANCOVA
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Residuals vs Fitted: check for non-linearity and unequal variance
plot(model_base, which = 1,
     main   = "Residuals vs Fitted",
     sub    = "Look for: random scatter (no curve, no funnel shape)")

# Normal Q-Q: check whether residuals are approximately normal
plot(model_base, which = 2,
     main   = "Normal Q-Q",
     sub    = "Look for: points close to the diagonal line")







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))







Note



Reading the diagnostic plots:

Residuals vs Fitted (left): The residuals should scatter randomly above and below zero with no systematic curve and no funnel shape (which would indicate variance increasing with fitted values). A smooth red line near zero is a good sign.
Normal Q-Q (right): The standardized residuals should fall approximately on the diagonal line. Some deviation at the tails is acceptable in small samples; systematic curvature throughout the plot would indicate non-normality.

For the IVAM-ED simulation, both plots should look acceptable. The SRQ-20 is a bounded integer score with some right skew — slight departures from normality in the Q-Q plot tails are expected and not cause for concern with n = 103.

6.6 3. Adjusted Means
The ANCOVA model produces adjusted means — the estimated group means at follow-up after accounting for baseline differences. These are what the paper reports in Table 2 as “Adjusted mean (SE)”.
The adjusted means are evaluated at the grand mean of the baseline covariate (not the group-specific mean). This removes the effect of any baseline imbalance.

# Grand mean of baseline SRQ-20 across all completers
grand_mean_srq20 <- mean(completers$srq20_0)
cat("Grand mean of baseline SRQ-20:", round(grand_mean_srq20, 2), "\n\n")

Grand mean of baseline SRQ-20: 7.19 

# Adjusted means: predict at grand mean of baseline, for each group

  model_base,
  newdata = data.frame(
    group   = c(0, 1),
    srq20_0 = c(grand_mean_srq20, grand_mean_srq20)
  ),
  se.fit = TRUE
)

    round(adj_means$fit[1], 2), "(", round(adj_means$se.fit[1], 2), ")\n")

6.8 5. Replicating Table 2: All Outcomes
The paper’s Table 2 reports baseline-adjusted and fully adjusted results for all five outcomes. Here we fit the baseline-adjusted model for each and compile the results.

# Helper: fit ANCOVA for one outcome and return a tidy summary row
ancova_row <- function(data, outcome_12, outcome_0, label) {
  fmla <- as.formula(paste(outcome_12, "~", "group +", outcome_0))
  m    <- lm(fmla, data = data)
  ci   <- confint(m)["group", ]
  coef_row <- coef(summary(m))["group", ]

  data.frame(
    Outcome       = label,
    MD            = round(coef_row["Estimate"], 2),
    SE            = round(coef_row["Std. Error"], 2),
    `CI lower`    = round(ci[1], 2),
    `CI upper`    = round(ci[2], 2),
    `p-value`     = round(coef_row["Pr(>|t|)"], 3),
    check.names   = FALSE
  )
}

title: 7  Module 6: Missing Data
text:
7.1 Overview
Nine of 112 enrolled participants (8%) did not complete the 12-week follow-up. That is a modest rate — but how we handle those 9 participants can matter. This module examines three approaches to missing outcome data and compares their results.
By the end of this module you should be able to:

title: 7  Module 6: Missing Data
text:
Describe three missing-data mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and explain why the mechanism matters for analysis.
Conduct a complete-case analysis and state its assumptions.
Apply a baseline-observation-carried-forward (BOCF) sensitivity analysis.
Run a simple multiple-imputation analysis using the mice package and pool the results.
Interpret how much the estimates change across the three approaches.

title: 7  Module 6: Missing Data
text:
7.4 2. Missing Data Mechanisms
Before choosing an analysis approach, we need to think about why data are missing. There are three formal mechanisms:








Mechanism
Definition
Implication




MCAR (Missing Completely At Random)
Missingness is unrelated to any variable, observed or unobserved
Complete-case analysis is unbiased


MAR (Missing At Random)
Missingness depends on observed variables (e.g., baseline score) but not on the unobserved follow-up value
Multiple imputation or mixed models are valid


MNAR (Missing Not At Random)
Missingness depends on the unobserved follow-up value itself (e.g., those who got worse stopped coming)
No standard analysis is fully valid; sensitivity analyses needed



In the IVAM-ED protocol, the authors stated: “the frequency and reasons for missing data are expected to be missing at random (MAR).” The three deaths are arguably MCAR (unrelated to the outcome); the six lost-to-follow-up are assumed MAR.

title: 7  Module 6: Missing Data
text:
7.5 3. Analysis 1: Complete-Case Analysis
A complete-case analysis uses only the 103 participants with follow-up data and ignores the 9 who are missing. This is what we have been doing in modules 4 and 5. It is the simplest approach.
Assumption: The 103 completers are representative of all 112 enrolled participants — or more precisely, that missingness is independent of the follow-up outcome after conditioning on the observed baseline values (MAR).

completers <- filter(dat, missing_12wk == 0)

model_cca <- lm(srq20_12 ~ group + srq20_0, data = completers)

cca_coef <- coef(summary(model_cca))["group", ]
cca_ci   <- confint(model_cca)["group", ]

title: 7  Module 6: Missing Data
text:
7.6 4. Analysis 2: Baseline Observation Carried Forward (BOCF)
BOCF replaces each missing follow-up value with the participant’s own baseline value. This assumes that participants who dropped out had no change from baseline — a conservative assumption that tends to underestimate treatment effects.
The IVAM-ED SAP listed BOCF as one of the pre-specified sensitivity analyses (strategy 2: “a baseline observation carried forward approach”).

# Apply BOCF: if srq20_12 is missing, use srq20_0 as the follow-up value
dat_bocf <- dat |>
  mutate(
    srq20_12_bocf = if_else(is.na(srq20_12), srq20_0, srq20_12)
  )

model_bocf <- lm(srq20_12_bocf ~ group + srq20_0, data = dat_bocf)

bocf_coef <- coef(summary(model_bocf))["group", ]
bocf_ci   <- confint(model_bocf)["group", ]

cat("BOCF ANCOVA (n = 112):\n")

BOCF ANCOVA (n = 112):

cat(sprintf("  MD:    %.3f\n",   bocf_coef["Estimate"]))

  MD:    -1.200

cat(sprintf("  SE:    %.3f\n",   bocf_coef["Std. Error"]))

  SE:    0.421

cat(sprintf("  95%% CI: (%.2f, %.2f)\n", bocf_ci[1], bocf_ci[2]))

  95% CI: (-2.03, -0.36)

cat(sprintf("  p:     %.4f\n",   bocf_coef["Pr(>|t|)"]))

  p:     0.0053








Note



Why BOCF is conservative: By assuming no change for dropouts, BOCF adds observations that pull both groups’ follow-up means toward their baseline values. If dropouts tend to have higher baseline distress (as in our simulation), their imputed follow-up values will be higher than average, pushing both group means up and slightly reducing the between-group difference.

title: 7  Module 6: Missing Data
text:
7.7 5. Analysis 3: Multiple Imputation (MI)
Multiple imputation generates several (typically 5–20) plausible complete datasets by drawing imputed values from a model of the missing data, runs the analysis on each complete dataset, and combines the results using Rubin’s rules.
Under MAR, MI is statistically valid and more efficient than BOCF. The IVAM-ED SAP specified MI with baseline data correction as its primary missing-data strategy.

# Variables to include in the imputation model
# Including auxiliary variables (all baselines, demographics) helps MI
# produce better imputations.
vars_for_mi <- dat |>
  select(srq20_12, srq20_0, sf36_12, sf36_0, hba1c_12, hba1c_0,
         sci_r_12, sci_r_0, pss_12, pss_0,
         group, age, female, edu_years, income_wages, mmse_0)

# Run multiple imputation: 5 imputations, 10 iterations
# seed for reproducibility; method "pmm" = predictive mean matching for continuous vars
set.seed(241)
mi_imp <- mice(vars_for_mi, m = 5, maxit = 10, method = "pmm",
               printFlag = FALSE)


# Fit the ANCOVA on each imputed dataset and pool the results
mi_fit    <- with(mi_imp, lm(srq20_12 ~ group + srq20_0))
mi_pooled <- pool(mi_fit)

summary(mi_pooled, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == "group") |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, `2.5 %`, `97.5 %`, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

   term estimate std.error  2.5 % 97.5 % p.value
2 group   -1.171     0.439 -2.045 -0.298   0.009








Note



Reading MI output:

estimate: the treatment effect, averaged (pooled) across all 5 imputed datasets.
std.error: the pooled SE, which accounts for both within-imputation and between-imputation variability.
2.5 % and 97.5 %: the 95% CI from Rubin’s rules.

Because only 9 participants (8%) are missing, the three approaches should give very similar estimates. Large divergence would signal that the MAR assumption may not hold.

title: 7  Module 6: Missing Data
text:
7.8 6. Comparing the Three Approaches

# Gather results from all three analyses
mi_row <- summary(mi_pooled, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == "group")

sensitivity <- data.frame(
  Analysis = factor(
    c("Complete-case\n(n = 103)", "BOCF\n(n = 112)", "Multiple imputation\n(n = 112)"),
    levels = c("Complete-case\n(n = 103)", "BOCF\n(n = 112)", "Multiple imputation\n(n = 112)")
  ),
  MD = c(cca_coef["Estimate"],  bocf_coef["Estimate"],  mi_row$estimate),
  lo = c(cca_ci[1],             bocf_ci[1],             mi_row$`2.5 %`),
  hi = c(cca_ci[2],             bocf_ci[2],             mi_row$`97.5 %`)
)

ggplot(sensitivity, aes(x = MD, xmin = lo, xmax = hi, y = Analysis)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbarh(height = 0.2, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 4, shape = 18, color = "#4472C4") +
  labs(
    title   = "SRQ-20 Treatment Effect: Sensitivity to Missing Data Approach",
    x       = "Mean difference (Smart speaker − Usual care)",
    y       = NULL,
    caption = "All models baseline-adjusted (ANCOVA)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)














Note



What consistent results mean: If all three estimates point in the same direction and have overlapping confidence intervals, the primary conclusion is robust to the missing data assumptions. The published IVAM-ED paper reported that both BOCF and complete-case analyses were consistent with the primary MI analysis, supporting the robustness of the main result.

title: 8  Module 7: Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text:
8.3 1. Statistical Significance vs. Clinical Significance
A statistically significant result (p < 0.05) tells us the observed effect is unlikely to be due to chance. It says nothing about whether the effect is large enough to matter in practice.
Clinical significance asks: Is this effect large enough to benefit patients in a meaningful way?

8.3.1 1a. The minimum clinically important difference (MCID)
For the SRQ-20, the MCID — the smallest change a patient would notice and consider beneficial — is typically reported as 3 points in comparable populations. (Note: a formal MCID for this specific population may not be published; this is an instructive approximation.)

# Fit baseline-adjusted ANCOVA for primary outcome
model <- lm(srq20_12 ~ group + srq20_0, data = completers)
md    <- coef(model)["group"]
ci    <- confint(model)["group", ]

# Pooled SD for standardized effect size
pooled_sd <- completers |>
  summarise(sd = sd(srq20_0)) |>
  pull(sd)

cohens_d  <- md / pooled_sd

cat("SRQ-20 primary outcome:\n")

SRQ-20 primary outcome:

cat(sprintf("  Baseline-adjusted MD:  %.2f points\n", md))

  Baseline-adjusted MD:  -1.19 points

cat(sprintf("  95%% CI:                (%.2f, %.2f)\n", ci[1], ci[2]))

  95% CI:                (-2.06, -0.32)

cat(sprintf("  Pooled baseline SD:    %.2f\n", pooled_sd))

  Pooled baseline SD:    3.81

cat(sprintf("  Cohen's d:             %.2f\n", cohens_d))

  Cohen's d:             -0.31

cat(sprintf("\n  MCID threshold (approximate): 3 points\n"))


  MCID threshold (approximate): 3 points

cat(sprintf("  Does the MD exceed the MCID?  %s\n",
    ifelse(abs(md) >= 3, "Yes", "No — upper CI does not reach MCID")))

  Does the MD exceed the MCID?  No — upper CI does not reach MCID








Warning



A statistically significant but clinically modest effect. The adjusted MD is approximately −1.2 to −1.5 points on a 20-point scale. The 95% CI’s upper bound is close to zero, and neither the point estimate nor the CI upper bound reaches the approximate 3-point MCID. The result is statistically significant but the clinical magnitude is modest.
This is a common pattern in trials with modest effect sizes and limited power: the study is large enough to detect the effect as real but the effect itself may not be large enough to change clinical practice on its own. The authors acknowledged this limitation and noted the trial was designed with an effect size of 0.68 — the observed effect may have been smaller.




8.3.2 1b. Visualizing the CI against the MCID

mcid <- -3   # negative because lower SRQ-20 = better

ggplot(data.frame(MD = md, lo = ci[1], hi = ci[2]),
       aes(x = MD, xmin = lo, xmax = hi, y = 1)) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = -Inf, xmax = mcid, ymin = 0.5, ymax = 1.5),
            fill = "#E2EFDA", alpha = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = mcid - 0.1, y = 1.35,
           label = "MCID\nthreshold", hjust = 1, size = 3.2, color = "#538135") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0,    linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mcid, linetype = "dotted", color = "#538135", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbarh(height = 0.25, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 4, shape = 18, color = "#4472C4") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-4, 1), breaks = seq(-4, 1, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.3, 1.6)) +
  labs(
    title   = "SRQ-20 Treatment Effect vs. Approximate Minimum Clinically Important Difference",
    x       = "Mean difference (Smart speaker − Usual care)",
    y       = NULL,
    caption = "Green shaded region = effects that meet or exceed the approximate MCID of 3 points"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())

title: 8  Module 7: Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text:
8.4 2. Primary vs. Exploratory Findings
The IVAM-ED protocol pre-specified one primary outcome (SRQ-20 at 12 weeks) and five secondary outcomes (SF-36, SCI-R, PSS, HbA1c, and blood pressure). Only the primary outcome was powered for confirmatory inference.
The secondary outcomes were described as exploratory because: - The trial was not powered to detect effects on secondary outcomes. - Multiple outcomes were tested without adjustment for multiple comparisons. - Exploratory findings generate hypotheses for future trials; they do not confirm effects.

# Reproduce Table 2 from Module 5 and label the outcomes
ancova_row <- function(data, y12, y0, label, type) {
  m  <- lm(as.formula(paste(y12, "~ group +", y0)), data = data)
  ci <- confint(m)["group", ]
  coef_row <- coef(summary(m))["group", ]
  data.frame(
    Outcome = label, Type = type,
    MD      = round(coef_row["Estimate"], 2),
    `95% CI`= paste0("(", round(ci[1], 2), ", ", round(ci[2], 2), ")"),
    p       = round(coef_row["Pr(>|t|)"], 3),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

bind_rows(
  ancova_row(completers, "srq20_12", "srq20_0", "SRQ-20",  "Primary (confirmatory)"),
  ancova_row(completers, "sf36_12",  "sf36_0",  "SF-36",   "Secondary (exploratory)"),
  ancova_row(completers, "sci_r_12", "sci_r_0", "SCI-R",   "Secondary (exploratory)"),
  ancova_row(completers, "pss_12",   "pss_0",   "PSS",     "Secondary (exploratory)"),
  ancova_row(completers, "hba1c_12", "hba1c_0", "HbA1c %", "Secondary (exploratory)")
)

title: 8  Module 7: Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text:
8.5 3. Multiple Comparisons
When you test five outcomes at α = 0.05, the probability of getting at least one false positive (by chance alone) is:
\[1 - (1 - 0.05)^5 = 1 - 0.95^5 \approx 0.226\]
That is, even if none of the interventions have a true effect on the secondary outcomes, we expect about a 23% chance of seeing at least one p < 0.05 among the five tests just by random variation.

8.5.1 3a. Bonferroni correction
The simplest multiplicity correction is Bonferroni: divide the target α by the number of tests. With 5 tests, the corrected threshold is 0.05 / 5 = 0.01.

results_all <- bind_rows(
  ancova_row(completers, "srq20_12", "srq20_0", "SRQ-20",  "Primary"),
  ancova_row(completers, "sf36_12",  "sf36_0",  "SF-36",   "Secondary"),
  ancova_row(completers, "sci_r_12", "sci_r_0", "SCI-R",   "Secondary"),
  ancova_row(completers, "pss_12",   "pss_0",   "PSS",     "Secondary"),
  ancova_row(completers, "hba1c_12", "hba1c_0", "HbA1c %", "Secondary")
)

results_all |>
  mutate(
    `Sig at α = 0.05`   = ifelse(p < 0.05,    "Yes", "No"),
    `Sig at α = 0.01\n(Bonferroni)` = ifelse(p < 0.01, "Yes", "No")
  )

             Outcome      Type    MD         95% CI     p Sig at α = 0.05
Estimate...1  SRQ-20   Primary -1.19 (-2.06, -0.32) 0.008             Yes
Estimate...2   SF-36 Secondary  5.95  (0.05, 11.85) 0.048             Yes
Estimate...3   SCI-R Secondary  1.39  (-0.48, 3.26) 0.142              No
Estimate...4     PSS Secondary -3.28 (-6.39, -0.16) 0.040             Yes
Estimate...5 HbA1c % Secondary -0.54 (-0.96, -0.12) 0.012             Yes
             Sig at α = 0.01\n(Bonferroni)
Estimate...1                           Yes
Estimate...2                            No
Estimate...3                            No
Estimate...4                            No
Estimate...5                            No








Note



What the Bonferroni correction shows: The primary outcome (SRQ-20) should remain significant under the corrected threshold if p < 0.01. Some secondary outcomes that were significant at 0.05 may no longer meet the stricter threshold. This illustrates why exploratory secondary findings require cautious interpretation and should be labeled as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.

title: 8  Module 7: Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text:
8.6 4. Protocol-to-Publication Comparison
One of the most important skills in evidence-based medicine is comparing what was done (published paper) to what was planned (protocol and SAP).
The IVAM-ED protocol was published in Trials in 2024 (Da Costa et al.) before the results were available. The results paper was published in JAMA Network Open in 2026. Both are in source/extracted/.

8.6.1 4a. Changes found between the protocol and the publication
Below are four specific changes that a careful reader can identify by comparing the two documents. Read the relevant sections in source/extracted/ to verify each one.

# This code block is a structured record — not analysis output.
# It serves as a reference table for the discussion below.
changes <- data.frame(
  `Change #` = 1:4,
  Feature    = c(
    "Age subgroup cutoff",
    "Education subgroup category",
    "History of anxiety subgroup",
    "Secondary outcome p-values"
  ),
  `Protocol/SAP specified` = c(
    "Age ≥ 80 years as the cutoff for the older-age subgroup",
    "Graduate education (vs. lower) as the subgroup category",
    "Not pre-specified",
    "P-values for secondary outcomes would NOT be reported (exploratory)"
  ),
  `Published` = c(
    "Age ≥ 75 years — changed because too few participants were aged ≥ 80",
    "Secondary education (vs. primary/none) — changed because too few had graduate degrees",
    "Added post hoc; history of anxiety had high prevalence (33.9%) in the sample",
    "P-values reported for all secondary outcomes in Table 2"
  ),
  `SAP language` = c(
    "\"The age cutoff was originally set at 80 years, but this was changed to 75 years due to the low number of participants aged 80 years or older.\" (Results paper)",
    "\"The educational-level category was adjusted from graduate to secondary education.\" (Results paper)",
    "\"An additional unplanned analysis of history of anxiety was included due to its high prevalence.\" (Results paper)",
    "SAP states secondary outcomes are exploratory; results paper reports p-values in Table 2 without explicit multiplicity disclaimer in the table"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

# Print with reasonable formatting
for (i in seq_len(nrow(changes))) {
  cat(sprintf("Change %d: %s\n", i, changes$Feature[i]))
  cat(sprintf("  Planned:   %s\n", changes$`Protocol/SAP specified`[i]))
  cat(sprintf("  Published: %s\n", changes$Published[i]))
  cat(sprintf("  Evidence:  %s\n\n", changes$`SAP language`[i]))
}

Change 1: Age subgroup cutoff
  Planned:   Age ≥ 80 years as the cutoff for the older-age subgroup
  Published: Age ≥ 75 years — changed because too few participants were aged ≥ 80
  Evidence:  "The age cutoff was originally set at 80 years, but this was changed to 75 years due to the low number of participants aged 80 years or older." (Results paper)

Change 2: Education subgroup category
  Planned:   Graduate education (vs. lower) as the subgroup category
  Published: Secondary education (vs. primary/none) — changed because too few had graduate degrees
  Evidence:  "The educational-level category was adjusted from graduate to secondary education." (Results paper)

Change 3: History of anxiety subgroup
  Planned:   Not pre-specified
  Published: Added post hoc; history of anxiety had high prevalence (33.9%) in the sample
  Evidence:  "An additional unplanned analysis of history of anxiety was included due to its high prevalence." (Results paper)

Change 4: Secondary outcome p-values
  Planned:   P-values for secondary outcomes would NOT be reported (exploratory)
  Published: P-values reported for all secondary outcomes in Table 2
  Evidence:  SAP states secondary outcomes are exploratory; results paper reports p-values in Table 2 without explicit multiplicity disclaimer in the table




8.6.2 4b. Are these changes problematic?
Not all protocol deviations are equal. Consider each on a spectrum:
Pre-specified but pragmatically adjusted (low concern): The age and education subgroup cutoff changes were both driven by the actual sample composition — there were simply too few participants in the original categories to analyze. The authors disclosed these changes explicitly in the Results section. This is transparent post-hoc adaptation, not hidden manipulation.
Added post hoc (moderate concern): The history of anxiety subgroup was not pre-specified. The authors added it because anxiety had a high prevalence in their sample and the effect appeared notable. This is a legitimate scientific observation but it means the reported subgroup finding has a higher false-positive rate than a pre-specified subgroup. It should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating.
Reporting practice inconsistency (moderate concern): The SAP described secondary outcomes as exploratory and noted that p-values for secondary outcomes would not serve as the basis for conclusions. Yet p-values are reported in Table 2 without an explicit “exploratory only” label on each row. A reader who does not consult the SAP may treat the secondary p-values as confirmatory tests. The Methods section does note the exploratory nature, but the table itself does not.






Important



The broader lesson: Even well-conducted, transparently reported trials in prestigious journals contain protocol deviations. This is normal — clinical research requires pragmatic adaptation. The critical-appraisal skill is to identify and evaluate these deviations, not to condemn the study for having them. A deviation disclosed in the paper is far less concerning than a deviation you discover only by reading the protocol.
